denomProfiles/church-of-greece/tagline: The autocephalous Orthodox church of most of Greece, the nation's 'prevailing religion'.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/coreDoctr: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith; doctrine is set by the Ecumenical Councils and Holy Tradition.
The Greek constitution (Article 3) names the Eastern Orthodox Church of Christ the 'prevailing religion' and binds it dogmatically to Constantinople.
Its Charter requires the Holy Synod to preserve unity of faith with the Ecumenical Patriarchate and the other Orthodox churches.
Treats the Greek-language New Testament and the Septuagint as the Church's authoritative biblical text.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/focuses/0: Close bonds between Orthodoxy and Greek national identity since the War of Independence (1821).
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/focuses/1: Lay renewal movements such as Zoe (1907) and Apostoliki Diakonia, the church's mission and publishing arm.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/focuses/2: A theological revival from the 1960s, associated with thinkers such as Christos Yannaras.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/focuses/3: Social welfare through parishes, especially during the economic crisis after 2010.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/practices: Byzantine liturgy in Koine Greek with Byzantine chant; name days are widely celebrated.
Adopted the Revised Julian calendar in 1924, prompting the Old Calendarist schism.
Holy Week and Pascha are national festivals, with the midnight 'Christos anesti' and candlelit processions.
Governed by the Archbishop of Athens and All Greece with the Holy Synod; clergy salaries have long been paid by the state.
Crete and the Dodecanese stay under Constantinople, and the northern 'New Lands' are administered by Athens on Constantinople's behalf (1928 Act).
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/influence: Churches of the Genuine Orthodox Christians separated in protest at the 1924 calendar change.
Greek-trained clergy and the Greek missiologist Anastasios played a key role in its revival.
Greek theologians and missionary societies supported the African dioceses of the Patriarchate of Alexandria.
denomProfiles/church-of-greece/keyFigure: Editor of the Philokalia and the Pedalion (Rudder) of canon law.
Archbishop of Athens who introduced the Revised Julian calendar in 1924.
Archbishop (1998–2008) known for his public, national profile.
Archbishop of Athens and All Greece since 2008.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/taglin: Arabic-speaking Orthodox patriarchate of the city where disciples were first called Christians.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/coreDo: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith and the Chalcedonian Christology accepted at the Council of 451.
Claims succession from the apostle Peter and from Ignatius of Antioch at the see of Antioch.
Stresses a conciliar Orthodoxy open to its Arab cultural setting and to dialogue with Muslims.
Recognises the canonical territory of other Orthodox churches, and has defended its own in disputes, such as with Jerusalem over Qatar.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/focuse: Witness of Arab Christians in Syria and Lebanon amid war, emigration and kidnapping of clergy.
Youth and lay renewal through the Orthodox Youth Movement, founded in Lebanon in 1942.
Education, notably the University of Balamand in Lebanon (1988).
A large diaspora in the Americas and Australia, open to Western converts.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/practi: Byzantine liturgy in Arabic, with Greek and, in the diaspora, English.
The Patriarch has resided in Damascus since the 14th century.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
Its North American archdiocese received Evangelical Orthodox converts in 1987 and allows a Western Rite vicariate.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/influe: A pro-Catholic party separated in 1724 to form a Byzantine-rite church in communion with Rome.
Peter Gillquist's Evangelical Orthodox Church entered its North American archdiocese in 1987.
denomProfiles/antiochian-orthodox/keyFig: Early-2nd-century bishop and martyr, revered as a founding father of the see.
Antiochene priest and preacher before becoming Archbishop of Constantinople.
Metropolitan of Mount Lebanon and co-founder of the Orthodox Youth Movement.
Patriarch (1979–2012) and founder of the University of Balamand.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/tagli: Greek Orthodox patriarchate of St Mark, now chiefly a missionary church across Africa.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/coreD: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith, including the Chalcedonian definition rejected by the Coptic majority of Egypt.
Claims succession from the evangelist Mark and from Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria.
Claims jurisdiction over the whole of Africa, a claim tested since 2021 by Moscow's rival African exarchate.
In 2016 its synod decided to restore the female diaconate, an ancient order, consecrating deaconesses in the Congo in 2017.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/focus: Missionary growth in sub-Saharan Africa: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, the Congo, Nigeria and beyond.
Translation of the liturgy into African languages and training of African clergy.
Care for the remnant Greek communities of Egypt.
Schools, clinics and orphanages run through its African dioceses.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/pract: The Patriarch resides in Alexandria and bears the title Pope and Patriarch.
Byzantine liturgy in Greek, Arabic, English, French, Swahili, Luganda and other languages.
African dioceses grew from the 1920s movement of Reuben Spartas Mukasa in Uganda, received by Alexandria in 1946.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/influ: Its mission created Orthodox churches with African clergy and bishops in more than a dozen countries.
Its 2019 recognition of the OCU led Moscow to break communion and set up its own exarchate in Africa.
denomProfiles/alexandrian-orthodox/keyFi: 4th-century bishop and champion of Nicaea, revered by both Alexandrian patriarchates.
5th-century patriarch and theologian of the Council of Ephesus.
Ugandan founder of the Orthodox movement in East Africa.
Pope and Patriarch since 2004, who has emphasised African mission.
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/tagline: Mother Church of Jerusalem, guardian of the Holy Sepulchre and the holy places.
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/coreDoc: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Claims descent from the first Christian community led by James, the brother of the Lord.
Raised to a patriarchate at the Council of Chalcedon (451) under Bishop Juvenal.
Sees itself as custodian of the holy places on behalf of the whole Orthodox world.
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/focuses: Guardianship of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Church of the Nativity, shared under the Ottoman 'Status Quo'.
Pastoral care of Arabic-speaking Orthodox Christians in Israel, Palestine and Jordan.
Hospitality to pilgrims from across the Orthodox world.
Management of extensive church lands, a source of controversy over sales and leases.
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/practic: Its hierarchy is drawn from the Greek-speaking monastic Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, while most laity are Arab.
The ceremony of the Holy Fire on Holy Saturday at the tomb of Christ draws vast crowds.
The Patriarch consecrates the Archbishop of the autonomous Church of Mount Sinai (St Catherine's Monastery).
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/influen: Arab laity have campaigned since the late 19th century for a greater role in the patriarchate.
Liturgies of Jerusalem shaped the Church's year, including Holy Week and the stational liturgy described by Egeria.
denomProfiles/jerusalem-orthodox/keyFigu: Leader of the Jerusalem church, venerated as its first bishop.
4th-century bishop whose catechetical lectures describe the Jerusalem rites.
Patriarch who surrendered Jerusalem to the Caliph Umar in 638.
Patriarch since 2005, after the deposition of Irenaios I.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/tagline: Church of St Sava, bound up with Serbian identity and the monasteries of Kosovo.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/coreDoctr: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
'Svetosavlje', the spiritual legacy of St Sava, presents Orthodoxy and Serbian identity as deeply intertwined.
Venerates the 'Kosovo covenant', the choice of the heavenly over the earthly kingdom linked to the Battle of Kosovo (1389).
Teaching shaped by 20th-century theologians Justin Popović and Nikolaj Velimirović, both canonised.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/focuses/0: Preservation of medieval monasteries in Kosovo, such as Peć, Visoki Dečani and Gračanica (UNESCO sites).
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/focuses/1: Serbian communities across the former Yugoslavia, Montenegro and the diaspora.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/focuses/3: Remembrance of 20th-century suffering, including the Jasenovac camp in the Second World War.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/practices: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, increasingly also in Serbian.
Keeps the Julian calendar; Christmas on 7 January with the badnjak (Yule log).
The krsna slava, a family feast of its patron saint, is a distinctive household tradition.
Led by the Patriarch of Serbia, with his seat in Belgrade and the historic see at Peć.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/influence: The Ohrid Archbishopric, which declared autocephaly from Belgrade in 1967, was granted it by Serbia in 2022.
Its dioceses shape church life in Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia.
denomProfiles/serbian-orthodox/keyFigure: First Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian church (1219) and its patron saint.
Tsar who raised the archbishopric to a patriarchate in 1346.
Ascetic patriarch (1990–2009) through the Yugoslav wars.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/tagline: Orthodoxy of a Latin people: the second-largest Orthodox church in the world.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/coreDoct: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Its theology was renewed by Dumitru Stăniloae, whose Romanian Philokalia and Dogmatic Theology are classics.
Sees Orthodoxy as integral to Romanian identity while affirming religious freedom under the 1990s democratic order.
Emphasises a 'philokalic' tradition of prayer descending from Paisius Velichkovsky's revival at Neamț.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/focuses/: Rebuilding church life after communism, including thousands of new churches and the People's Salvation Cathedral in Bucharest (consecrated 2018).
Monastic life, with many monasteries in Moldavia and Bukovina.
Diaspora parishes for millions of Romanian emigrants in Western Europe.
Religious education in state schools and social work.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/practice: Byzantine liturgy in Romanian, in use since the 17th–18th centuries (Bucharest Bible, 1688).
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts (since 1924).
The painted monasteries of Bukovina, with exterior frescoes, are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Led by a Patriarch (since 1925) and a Holy Synod; Patriarch Daniel has served since 2007.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/influenc: Created by the 1700 union at Alba Iulia; forcibly absorbed into the Orthodox church in 1948 and restored in 1989–90.
Stăniloae's work on the Trinity and deification shaped Orthodox and ecumenical theology.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/keyFigur: 18th-century abbot of Neamț and reviver of hesychast prayer.
Patriarch (1948–77) who steered the church under communist rule.
The leading Romanian Orthodox theologian of the 20th century.
denomProfiles/romanian-orthodox/members/: Approximate number of people declaring Orthodox religion in Romania's 2021 census, roughly three-quarters of the population; excludes Moldova and the diaspora.
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/tagline: First Slavic national church, cradle of Slavonic letters and the Cyrillic script.
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/coreDoc: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Treasures the legacy of Cyril and Methodius and their disciples as the foundation of Slavonic Christianity.
Was declared schismatic by Constantinople in 1872 for 'phyletism' (organising the church by ethnicity); the schism ended in 1945.
Left the World Council of Churches in 1998, reflecting conservative suspicion of ecumenism.
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/focuses: Preserving Orthodoxy as part of Bulgarian national identity, especially after Ottoman and communist rule.
Monastic heritage, above all Rila Monastery, founded by John of Rila.
Restoring church life and unity after the 1992–2012 schism with an alternative synod.
Rebuilding parish life, religious education and monasteries after the communist period (1944–89).
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/practic: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic and Bulgarian.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts (since 1968).
Led by a Patriarch of Bulgaria and Metropolitan of Sofia; Daniil was elected in 2024.
Popular feasts such as St George's Day and the Epiphany diving for the cross in rivers.
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/influen: Slavonic books and clergy from Bulgaria helped form the church of Kyivan Rus.
The Ohrid literary school shaped Slavonic church life in Serbia and Macedonia.
The Preslav and Ohrid schools spread the Cyrillic and Glagolitic scripts across the Slavic world.
denomProfiles/bulgarian-orthodox/keyFigu: Ruler who converted Bulgaria to Christianity in the 860s.
Byzantine missionaries whose disciples brought Slavonic letters to Bulgaria.
Disciple of Methodius, bishop and teacher of thousands of Slavonic clergy.
14th-century patriarch, hesychast and reformer of Slavonic texts.
